title: Fairness and Machine Learning: Limitations and Opportunities
venue: MIT Press (Adaptive Computation and Machine Learning series)
harvard_reference: Barocas, S., Hardt, M. and Narayanan, A. (2023) Fairness and machine learning: limitations and opportunities. Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. Available at: https://fairmlbook.org/ (Accessed: 27 September 2026).
abstract_summary: An interdisciplinary textbook on fairness in algorithmic decision-making, published by MIT Press in 2023 and also released open access at fairmlbook.org. The nine chapters are: Introduction; When is automated decision making legitimate?; Classification; Relative notions of fairness; Causality; Understanding United States anti-discrimination law; Testing discrimination in practice; A broader view of discrimination; and Datasets. The Classification chapter formalises three statistical non-discrimination criteria for a score R, sensitive attribute A and target Y: independence (A independent of R; for binary classifiers also called demographic parity, statistical parity, group fairness, disparate impact), separation (R independent of A given Y; error-rate parity / equalized odds; equality of opportunity when restricted to false negatives) and sufficiency (Y independent of A given R; shown to be essentially equivalent to calibration by group). It then proves pairwise incompatibility propositions: independence and sufficiency cannot both hold when A and Y are dependent; independence and separation cannot both hold when Y is binary and both A and R are dependent on Y; separation and sufficiency cannot both hold when A and Y are dependent and the classifier has a nonzero false positive rate (or all events have positive probability). A section headed 'No fairness through unawareness' explains that dropping the sensitive attribute fails because sensitive attributes are generally redundant given the other features, so a learner finds a redundant encoding (proxy) of the attribute, illustrated with retinal photographs predicting gender, genomic ancestry markers, and web-visit features predicting gender.

claims_supported.claim: Fairness criteria such as independence (demographic parity), separation (equalised odds) and sufficiency (calibration) are formally defined and generally mutually exclusive; 'fairness through unawareness' fails because of redundant encodings (proxies).
claims_supported.where: Chapter 3 'Classification' (https://fairmlbook.org/classification.html). Definitions: sections 'Independence' (A independent of R; 'demographic parity' named as the binary-classifier case), 'Separation' (R independent of A given Y; 'equalized odds' named), 'Sufficiency' (Y independent of A given R; 'calibration by group implies sufficiency' and the two are described as essentially equivalent). Incompatibility: section 'Relationships between criteria', which states propositions that independence and sufficiency cannot both hold when A and Y are dependent; independence and separation cannot both hold when Y is binary and A and R are each dependent on Y; and separation and sufficiency cannot both hold when A and Y are dependent and the classifier has a nonzero false positive rate. Unawareness: section 'No fairness through unawareness', which states that sensitive attributes are generally redundant given the other features, so a classifier trained without the attribute finds a redundant encoding in terms of the other features (examples: retinal photographs, genomic ancestry markers, website-visit features). Caveat for the report: the book's result is pairwise incompatibility under non-degenerate conditions (A and Y dependent, non-trivial classifier), not a single three-way impossibility theorem; the wording 'generally mutually exclusive' is accurate provided the report signals those conditions.

verification_notes: Verified 2026-09-27. Existence and core metadata confirmed from three independent sources: (1) the authors' own site fairmlbook.org, whose recommended BibTeX gives title 'Fairness and Machine Learning: Limitations and Opportunities', authors Solon Barocas, Moritz Hardt and Arvind Narayanan, publisher MIT Press, year 2023; (2) the Open Library edition record OL48231196M (search.json and isbn endpoints): same title/subtitle/authors, publisher MIT Press, publish_date 2023, ISBN-13 9780262048613, ISBN-10 0262048612, pagination 320; (3) a published review of the book in The Reasoner 20(1), 2026, doi:10.54103/1757-0522/29851, citing it as MIT Press, 2023. A web search additionally surfaced the Amazon listing (ISBN 9780262048613, 'Adaptive Computation and Machine Learning series') and pages stating the hardcover appeared in December 2023; series and month are therefore from retail/secondary listings rather than the publisher's page. DOI: a Crossref search filtered on isbn:9780262048613 returned zero results, and the Crossref bibliographic search returned only a review of the book, so no DOI is registered for the book itself; the doi field is left empty deliberately. The MIT Press product page (mitpress.mit.edu/9780262048613) and direct.mit.edu returned HTTP 403, WorldCat and Library of Congress were bot-blocked, and Google Books and Semantic Scholar returned HTTP 429, so the publisher's own page could not be read; place of publication 'Cambridge, MA' in the Harvard reference is the MIT Press's standard imprint location and was not read from a fetched catalogue record. Volume/issue/page range are not applicable to a monograph and are left empty (Open Library gives a total extent of 320 pages). The claim was checked against the full text of the Classification chapter on fairmlbook.org, not just an abstract.
caveats: The book is a monograph with no registered DOI; cite the ISBN or the open-access URL instead. The open-access web edition (fairmlbook.org) and the MIT Press print edition have the same chapter structure, but page numbers for direct quotations should be taken from the print/PDF edition if the report needs them. Series name and December 2023 hardcover date come from retail listings, not the publisher page, so treat them as unconfirmed. When citing the mutual-exclusivity result, note it is pairwise and conditional (A and Y dependent; non-trivial classifier), not an unconditional three-way impossibility.
